why: RFC-0045's single embedded bake site: a `repr(C)`, 236-byte, pointer-free struct (magic "NRBC", version, set_flags, domain_id, `node_name[64]`, `locator[96]`, `namespace[64]`) emitted into the `.nros_boot_config` linker section. The governing constraint is RFC-0045's: a device is never told anything at startup. There is no argv to parse, no environment to read and (on the embedded targets) no filesystem to load a YAML from, so the identity a desktop node gets from `ros2 run --ros-args -r __node:=talker` has to be BAKED into the image at link time. rcl/rclc/rclcpp/rclrs have no counterpart to any of this for the same reason they have no counterpart to a linker script. The shape is chosen for two scenarios beyond `where does an image get its name`. First, ONE inspectable symbol instead of per-board lore -- before this, identity arrived four different ways in Rust alone (runtime `from_env`, a baked `Config` with a hardcoded `nros_app`, `option_env!`, and on NuttX a trait default that silently dropped the overlay). Second, fleet provisioning: fixed-size fields and a scannable magic mean a post-link tool can rewrite a unit's node name, locator and domain in a built binary, so one firmware build flashes a fleet with per-unit identity and no recompile. The same struct is mirrored byte-for-byte in `rclc/detail/boot_config.h` with static asserts on size and every offset, so the language a node is written in does not change the blob.
